home.title: The Fundraising Game
home.introduction: Get your board members involved in building and executing your organization's fundraising strategy.
paragraphs: Imagine walking into your next board meeting, and every board member comes prepared with answers to some very specific fundraising questions.

Each person has identified who they believe should fund your organization's mission, why those people have a strong reason to give, where to find them, how to attract them, how to raise money from them, what to ask for, how much to ask, and the role they would love to play to support fundraising.
Now imagine what that board meeting would look like.
Each board member presents their recommended fundraising audience and explains why they believe that audience should support your mission.
You all discuss their recommendations, examine the opportunities, and agree on the specific audiences your organization should focus on.
Maybe you agree on one audience. Maybe two. You might even agree to pursue all the audiences recommended.
The important thing is that you have collectively agreed on who your organization will raise money from and exactly how you intend to raise that money.
And before that meeting ends, every board member agrees on the role they will personally play in helping the organization reach those audiences and raise money from them.
Think about what that would mean for your organization.
Think about what it would mean for your board.
Your organization now has a fundraising strategy that identifies who should fund your mission, where to find them, how to attract them, what to ask them for, and how much to ask.
These are the core elements of a fundraising strategy.

And because your board members participated in developing and adopting that strategy, they understand how the organization intends to raise money. They also understand where they fit into the process and what they have agreed to do.
You have a fundraising strategy your board helped build, and board members who are ready to work with you to execute it.
That's what we want to help you accomplish with The Fundraising Game.
We've put together the questions, materials, and tools you need to take your board through this process.

You don't need to hire a professional facilitator. You can lead the process yourself. And if you would prefer to have a professional facilitate your session, we will make a fundraising professional with years of experience available to help.
biography: My name is Rooney A. My mission is to help you raise money exponentially. And maybe transform your board while doing so.
So far I've contributed to raising over $5m based on my strategy and the fundraising assets I create. I've also trained hundreds of nonprofit leaders and fundraisers on sustainable fundraising.

There are two ways we can support you to build a successful fundraising strategy for your organization. You can do it with me alone. This is usually faster, usually within 24 to 48 hours, or you can do it with your board, and still get my help of course. But this could happen as soon as your next board meeting.

The number one reason most organizations struggle to raise money is their fundraising strategy or approach. Once you get it right, with a little focus, time and resource investment, you will begin to see the returns in no time.
home.cta: Play The Fundraising Game With Your Board

how.title: Here's how The Fundraising Game works.

steps.heading: Answer the fundraising questions.
paragraphs: You begin by answering specific questions about who you believe should fund your mission and how your organization should raise money from them.

steps.heading: Invite your board members to play The Fundraising Game.
paragraphs: Each board member receives an invitation to answer the same questions independently.
This gives every member the opportunity to think about your organization's fundraising opportunities and recommend an approach before the meeting.

steps.heading: Play The Fundraising Game together at your next board meeting.
paragraphs: During your meeting, you review everyone's responses, discuss the recommended audiences, and agree on the fundraising strategy your organization will adopt.
The platform provides the materials and guidance to help you facilitate this group session.

steps.heading: Agree on each board member's responsibilities.
paragraphs: Before the session ends, each board member identifies and accepts the specific role they will play in executing the fundraising strategy you have collectively adopted.

steps.heading: Receive your fundraising strategy and individual board member portfolios.
paragraphs: After the meeting, your organization receives the written fundraising strategy you all agreed on.
Each board member also receives their own portfolio, outlining their responsibilities and providing the tools and guidance they need to carry out their role.
So everybody leaves that process knowing who your organization is raising money from, how the organization intends to raise that money, and exactly what they are responsible for doing.
And that is how you begin to turn your board from a group of people who attend meetings into a group of people actively working with you to fund your mission.
Are you ready to get your board members fundraising by your next board meeting?
Set your fundraising goal, answer the 5 top fundraising questions, invite your board members to answer as well, stroll into your next board meeting and lead your board to decide.
We will provide you every support you need to ensure the success of the process.

followups.subject: Bring your board into the fundraising conversation
followups.body: You recently explored The Fundraising Game. Your board can help identify who should fund your mission and agree on how to reach them. Return to see how you can prepare for that conversation at your next board meeting.

followups.subject: Give every board member a chance to contribute
followups.body: Each board member can bring a different perspective on your organization's fundraising opportunities. The Fundraising Game gives everyone the same questions before you meet, so you can discuss their ideas together.

followups.subject: Prepare for a useful fundraising discussion
followups.body: You can lead this process yourself. The questions, facilitation guide and shared meeting tools help your board discuss complete fundraising approaches and decide which ones to adopt.

followups.subject: Turn agreed ideas into clear responsibilities
followups.body: The process ends with the fundraising strategy your board adopted and individual portfolios based on the responsibilities people actually agreed to undertake. You can review how it works before deciding to start.

followups.subject: Would you like to play The Fundraising Game with your board?
followups.body: If getting your board involved in fundraising is still a priority, you can return to The Fundraising Game whenever you are ready. It costs $497 once for your organization. This is the last email in this follow-up series.
